The Moral Imperative of Legalized Assisted Dying for Terminal and Severe Conditions

A Utilitarian and Compassionate Framework

Introduction

Among the most profound failures of modern civilization is our collective willingness to watch human beings suffer unnecessarily — sometimes for months or years — while hiding behind moral frameworks that prioritize abstract principles over lived agony. The legalization and thoughtful implementation of assisted dying for individuals with terminal illnesses or severe, irreversible conditions is not merely a policy option worth considering; it is an ethical obligation that follows from any serious commitment to human dignity, autonomy, and the reduction of suffering. This essay argues firmly in favor of robust legal frameworks for assisted dying, drawing on utilitarian reasoning, empirical evidence from jurisdictions that have already implemented such policies, and foundational principles of individual liberty.

A critical clarification at the outset: the argument here is for voluntary assisted dying with strong safeguards — not for any system where the state decides who lives or dies without consent. The word "mandate" in this context should refer to the government's obligation to make this option available, not to impose death on anyone. This distinction is essential, and maintaining it is what separates a compassionate policy from a dystopian one.

The Utilitarian Calculus of Suffering

Utilitarianism, in its most defensible forms, asks us to maximize well-being and minimize suffering across all affected parties. When we apply this framework rigorously to the situation of individuals dying slowly from terminal cancer, advanced ALS, end-stage organ failure, or other conditions where medicine can extend biological life but cannot restore meaningful quality of life, the calculation is stark.

Consider the experience of a patient with metastatic pancreatic cancer. The median survival after diagnosis is approximately six months. During much of this time, the patient may experience unrelenting pain, nausea, cachexia, psychological terror, and progressive loss of every capacity that made life meaningful to them. Modern palliative care, despite genuine advances, cannot fully alleviate suffering in all cases. Studies consistently show that somewhere between 10 and 30 percent of patients with terminal illness experience refractory symptoms — suffering that does not respond adequately to any available palliative intervention.

For these individuals, every additional day may represent not a gift but a sentence. The utilitarian must ask: what is the aggregate suffering produced by forcing — through legal prohibition — thousands of people annually to endure weeks or months of agony they desperately wish to escape? And what is the countervailing benefit? If the answer to the second question is merely that we have preserved an abstract principle about the sanctity of life — a principle the suffering person themselves rejects — then the utilitarian equation is not close. The concrete, experienced suffering of real human beings outweighs abstract commitments that those same humans do not wish to be bound by.

Jeremy Bentham's felicific calculus considered intensity, duration, certainty, and extent of pleasure and pain. Terminal suffering scores horrifyingly high on every dimension of pain: it is intense, prolonged, virtually certain, and affects not only the patient but an entire circle of loved ones who witness the deterioration. A policy that provides a peaceful exit reduces suffering across all of these dimensions simultaneously.

The Evidence from Existing Jurisdictions

We are not arguing in a vacuum. Multiple jurisdictions have implemented assisted dying with extensive track records that we can evaluate. Oregon's Death with Dignity Act has been in effect since 1997 — over a quarter century of data. The Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Canada, Colombia, several Australian states, and Switzerland all have legal frameworks permitting some form of assisted dying.

The empirical evidence from these jurisdictions consistently refutes the parade of horribles that opponents predicted:

The "slippery slope" has not materialized in the way critics feared. In Oregon, assisted deaths consistently represent approximately 0.4% of all deaths annually. After 25 years, the law has not expanded to encompass vulnerable populations being pressured into death. The overwhelming majority of those who use the law are well-educated, insured individuals with strong support systems who are making autonomous decisions about their own deaths.

Palliative care has actually improved. One of the most counterintuitive findings is that jurisdictions legalizing assisted dying often see improvements in palliative care rather than its erosion. Oregon consistently ranks among the top states for palliative care quality. The conversation around end-of-life options appears to enhance rather than diminish attention to comfort care. The legalization forces healthcare systems to take dying seriously.

Safeguards work. In Oregon, patients must make two oral requests separated by 15 days, provide a written request witnessed by two people, receive confirmation of their diagnosis and prognosis from two physicians, and be assessed for conditions such as depression that might impair judgment. Patients who receive prescriptions but choose not to use them — roughly one-third — demonstrate that having the option itself provides psychological comfort and a sense of control.

Abuse is extraordinarily rare. Multiple systematic reviews of Oregon and Dutch data have found no evidence of systematic abuse or disproportionate impact on disadvantaged populations. The regulatory frameworks have been remarkably effective at ensuring that assisted dying remains a carefully considered choice made by competent individuals.

Canada's Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID) program, while more recently implemented and more broadly scoped, provides additional evidence that a well-regulated system can function effectively. Since 2016, MAID has provided thousands of Canadians with a peaceful death they explicitly requested, and the system includes multiple layers of assessment and oversight.

Autonomy as a Foundational Value

The liberal democratic tradition rests on a fundamental commitment: competent adults have the right to make decisions about their own bodies and lives, particularly when those decisions affect primarily themselves. John Stuart Mill's harm principle — that the only legitimate reason for society to restrict individual liberty is to prevent harm to others — applies with exceptional force to end-of-life decisions.

When a terminally ill patient of sound mind concludes that continued existence represents unbearable suffering and requests medical assistance in dying, on what grounds does the state override that decision? The patient is not harming others. The patient has weighed their own values, their own experience of suffering, their own understanding of what makes life worth living, and has reached a conclusion. To tell this person, "No, you must continue to suffer because we have decided your life has value you yourself do not perceive" is an act of breathtaking paternalism.

This paternalism is particularly galling because it is selective. We respect patient autonomy in virtually every other medical context. Patients may refuse life-saving treatment, disconnect ventilators, decline chemotherapy, and sign do-not-resuscitate orders. A Jehovah's Witness may refuse a blood transfusion that would save their life, and we respect that decision. Yet when a patient asks for active assistance in dying — often a far more considered and deliberate choice than any of these — we suddenly discover limits to autonomy. The inconsistency is intellectually indefensible.

Moreover, the autonomy argument extends to individuals with severe, irreversible disabilities — though here we must be especially careful. The argument is emphatically not that disability makes life not worth living. Millions of people with severe disabilities live rich, fulfilling lives, and any suggestion that they should choose death is offensive and wrong. The argument is rather that some individuals with conditions involving unrelenting, treatment-resistant suffering — locked-in syndrome with full awareness, certain progressive neurological conditions, intractable chronic pain syndromes — should have the right to make their own assessment of whether continued life, as they experience it, is acceptable to them. No one else can make that judgment, because no one else inhabits their body or experiences their suffering.

The Societal Cost Argument — Handled Honestly

Critics often charge that cost-based arguments for assisted dying are dangerous — that they risk creating pressure on vulnerable individuals to die so as not to be a "burden." This concern is legitimate and must be taken seriously. But it is also important to be honest about the reality of end-of-life healthcare costs, not because these costs should ever be the primary justification for assisted dying, but because acknowledging resource realities is part of honest policy analysis.

Approximately 25% of Medicare spending in the United States occurs in the last year of life, and a significant portion of that spending occurs in the final month. Much of this expenditure funds interventions that do not meaningfully extend life or improve its quality — ICU stays for patients who will never recover, aggressive chemotherapy with marginal expected benefit, surgical procedures on individuals who are actively dying. This spending represents not just a financial cost but a human one: patients subjected to painful, invasive procedures that serve no purpose they would endorse if fully informed.

A system that provides assisted dying as an option — alongside excellent palliative care, honest prognostic conversations, and comprehensive support services — would likely reduce some of this spending. But the savings are a secondary benefit, not the primary justification. The primary justification remains the reduction of human suffering. Any policy framework must include ironclad safeguards ensuring that no individual ever feels economic pressure to choose death — this means robust social safety nets, universal access to palliative care, and strict separation between cost considerations and individual medical decisions.

The broader societal benefits, however, extend beyond direct cost savings. Family caregivers of terminally ill patients experience profound physical, emotional, and financial strain. Depression, anxiety, complicated grief, and caregiver burnout are endemic. When a loved one's death is prolonged and agonizing, the psychological toll on survivors can be devastating and lasting. A peaceful, chosen death — surrounded by family, at a moment the patient selects — can transform the experience of bereavement. Research from Oregon and other jurisdictions suggests that family members of patients who use assisted dying experience less traumatic grief and are more likely to feel that their loved one's end-of-life experience was consistent with their values.

Healthcare professionals also benefit. Physicians and nurses who witness prolonged, futile suffering experience moral distress — the anguish of knowing that they could help a patient achieve a peaceful death but are legally prohibited from doing so. This moral distress contributes to burnout and attrition in precisely the specialties (oncology, palliative care, geriatrics) where experienced clinicians are most needed.

Addressing Objections

"The sanctity of life." This argument, typically rooted in religious conviction, holds that human life is inherently sacred and that intentionally ending it is always wrong. This view deserves respect as a personal moral commitment, but it cannot serve as the basis for public policy in a pluralistic society. The person who holds this belief is free to decline assisted dying. They are not entitled to impose their metaphysical commitments on others who do not share them. In a society that separates church and state, policy must be justified by reasons accessible to all citizens, not by theological premises that many reject.

"Doctors should heal, not kill." The medical profession's commitment to non-maleficence — "first, do no harm" — is important but cannot be understood simplistically. Forcing a patient to endure months of unrelievable suffering is itself a harm. The physician who provides a peaceful death at a patient's explicit, repeated, competently expressed request is not violating the spirit of medical ethics; they are fulfilling it. They are responding to suffering when no other response remains. The medical associations of multiple countries have come to recognize this, and physician participation is always voluntary — no doctor who objects is compelled to participate.

"We should improve palliative care instead." This presents a false dichotomy. We should improve palliative care and provide assisted dying. These are complementary, not competing, approaches. Even the world's best palliative care cannot eliminate all suffering for all patients. As noted above, refractory symptoms are a reality that no amount of funding or innovation has fully solved. Palliative care specialists themselves — those closest to the reality of terminal suffering — are frequently among the most thoughtful advocates for assisted dying as a complement to their work.

"Vulnerable populations will be pressured." This concern deserves the most serious engagement because protecting vulnerable people is non-negotiable. But the evidence from existing jurisdictions provides strong reassurance. Robust safeguards — multiple requests over time, independent physician assessments, mental health evaluations, mandatory waiting periods, judicial review in contested cases — can and do protect against abuse. The question is not whether any conceivable system could be abused (any system can), but whether a well-designed system with strong safeguards produces better outcomes than the status quo. Given that the status quo involves thousands of people suffering unnecessarily, the bar for maintaining prohibition is high.

"People with disabilities will be devalued." Disability rights organizations have raised important concerns about the message that assisted dying laws send. These concerns must be honored in how we design and discuss these policies. The answer is not to deny autonomy to individuals who are suffering, but to simultaneously strengthen disability rights, ensure that all individuals with disabilities have access to the services and supports that make fulfilling lives possible, and make absolutely clear that assisted dying is about respecting choices — not about judging lives. The disability community is not monolithic on this issue; many individuals with severe disabilities are themselves advocates for the right to choose.

The Case for Government Implementation

Why should the government be involved at all? Why not simply allow private arrangements? The answer is that government involvement is essential precisely to protect the values opponents care about. Without a legal framework, assisted dying happens anyway — through illegal means, through the "double effect" of escalating opioid doses, through voluntary cessation of eating and drinking (a slow and sometimes distressing process), and through violent suicide. Estimates suggest that hundreds of terminally ill Americans end their lives through unregulated means annually.

A government-regulated system brings transparency, accountability, data collection, and oversight. It ensures that decisions are documented, that safeguards are followed, that vulnerable individuals are protected, and that the practice can be monitored and adjusted over time. The alternative to regulated assisted dying is not no assisted dying — it is unregulated, invisible, and potentially unsafe assisted dying.

Government implementation should include:

  • Universal access to palliative care as a prerequisite and companion to assisted dying
  • Mandatory waiting periods and multiple assessments to ensure decisions are stable and informed
  • Independent oversight bodies to review cases and identify any patterns of concern
  • Robust data collection and public reporting to enable ongoing evaluation
  • Conscientious objection provisions for healthcare providers who oppose participation
  • Comprehensive public education to ensure patients understand all options
  • Strong anti-coercion provisions with criminal penalties for anyone who pressures a vulnerable person

Conclusion

The question before us is not whether people will die — they will — but whether they will die with agency, dignity, and minimal suffering, or whether they will die in agony, stripped of control, subjected to the moral convictions of others who will never inhabit their bodies or experience their pain.

The utilitarian calculation is clear: a well-regulated system of assisted dying reduces aggregate suffering enormously while imposing minimal costs on those who choose not to participate. The autonomy argument is clear: competent adults have a fundamental right to make decisions about their own dying. The empirical evidence is clear: existing systems work, safeguards hold, and the feared abuses have not materialized.

To refuse to implement such a system — in the face of this evidence and these arguments — is to make a deliberate choice to perpetuate suffering. It is to look at a dying person begging for release and say, "My principles matter more than your pain." That is not moral courage. It is moral failure.

The time for legalized, carefully regulated, compassionately implemented assisted dying has arrived. Indeed, for the countless individuals who suffered and died without this option over decades of delay and debate, it arrived too late. We owe it to those who are suffering now — and those who will suffer in the future — to act with both compassion and resolve.

Note: This essay argues for voluntary assisted dying with robust safeguards. The author recognizes that this is a topic involving deeply held values on multiple sides, and that any implementation must center patient autonomy, protect vulnerable populations, and be accompanied by excellent palliative care for all.
